# Full Send

If the user triggered this, it's because they are not watching this thread, and
they want you to complete the work end-to-end autonomously. Your updates and
your final message go unread until long after you stop. You own the work from
its current state to a merged PR.

If the user did not explicitly request "full send" in some clear way, do not
assume full autonomy. If they did, everything below applies.

The user grants you permission to:

- Merge the PR once the merge gate passes.
- Force-push the PR's own branch with `--force-with-lease` after a rebase.
- Use the test methods that Proof needs, without asking first.

## Testing permission

A "full send" request is the permission. If a project file or other
instruction says to ask before a test method, or to leave testing to the
user, this request replaces that rule for this task.

That includes ask-first rules for computer use, browser automation,
simulators and devices, running the app or a dev server, screenshots, and
visual checks. Use the method that gives direct proof. List it in the
report.

Rules about how to test still apply. Follow rules that name the correct
command, fixture, or check. This permission only removes the ask-first or
leave-it-to-the-user step. If a preferred method cannot prove the change,
use a gated method under this permission.

It covers only the tests needed for this task. It does not add permission
for the steps under "Asking the user", such as production changes or data
deletion. It also does not bypass a harness or system approval prompt if
one appears.

## Steps

1. **Finish the change.** Complete the goal from the user's request with the
   smallest change that works. Fix the case that happened, not every case
   that could. If you are on the default branch, create a branch first.
2. **Prove it.** Get proof for every change you made. See "Proof".
3. **Get feedback.** Use the `sol-loop` skill to verify changes.
4. **File the PR** with the `file-pr` skill. Rebase onto the latest default
   branch first. Add one short line to the description that says how you proved
   the change.
5. **Babysit the PR** with the `babysit-pr` skill. Fix real findings and CI
   failures. Get proof for each fix before you push it.
6. **Merge** when the merge gate passes.
7. **Report** in your final message: the PR link, the merge commit, your proof,
   and each decision you made for the user.

Stay active from step 1 to step 7. If you end your turn while checks or bots are
pending, the work stops, because nobody will prompt you again. Wait with the
watcher from `babysit-pr`, so something wakes you when the PR changes. In T3
Code that is `watch_pull_request`. If you stop before the merge, call
`unwatch_pull_request` first.

## Proof

Proof is evidence you observed yourself in this session: command output, a
reproduction, a screenshot. Use the most direct proof the change allows:

- Reproduce the original failure, apply the fix, then watch the same
  reproduction pass.
- Run the checks that the repo's CI runs (typecheck, lint, tests).
- Add one focused test that fails without the fix, when the behavior has none
  and the repo has a test setup.
- For UI and runtime behavior, run the app and look at the change. Green mocked
  tests do not prove that the user experience works. Attach screenshots to the
  PR when they help and you have a way to upload them.

When you cannot find a way to prove a change, you do not have full confidence.
Ask the user.

## Merge gate

Full confidence means all of these are true on the latest commit:

- Your proof covers every change in the diff.
- Required checks are green.
- Review bots have finished, and each finding is fixed or dismissed with a
  written reason.
- No human review still requests changes.
- The branch is up to date with the default branch, and GitHub reports it as
  mergeable.

Merge with the method the repo uses. Check the allowed methods and recent merged
PRs. If the repo uses a merge queue or auto-merge, stay until GitHub reports the
PR as merged. Merge through branch protection as configured. Never use `--admin`
or other bypasses. You can ignore automated reviews that request "needs human
review" if you have high confidence in your changes.

## Asking the user

A question in a normal message goes unseen, and the thread looks done. To ask
the user something, use the harness's question tool so the thread shows that
it is waiting: `AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code, `request_user_input` in Codex,
or the question tool your harness has. Put all the context in the question:
the PR link, what blocks you, and the options with your recommendation first.

Ask only when you cannot continue alone:

- You cannot prove the change.
- The merge gate cannot pass, and you cannot fix that yourself.
- The next step is outside the grant above: deleting data, touching production,
  changing things outside the repo, closing a PR, or force-pushing any other
  branch.
- The goal is ambiguous in a way that changes the result.
- Another PR makes this one obsolete.

Decide everything else yourself with sensible defaults, and list those decisions
in the report.

If no question tool is available, or the tool returns no answer, take the safe
path: leave the PR open and unmerged, and start your final message with the
question.
SKILL.md

content.thinking:
This is a large undertaking, so I need to first survey the codebase carefully—the electron directory, build setup, tests, and how the main process currently loads .mjs files in the packaged app. I'm sketching a plan starting with converting the electron .mjs files to TypeScript with a proper build step, since package.json currently points to electron/main.mjs directly.

I'm weighing whether to keep source files as .ts and compile them per entry point (main, preload, workers) into dist/electron, which would mean the dev workflow needs a build step before launching electron. I also need to figure out native dependency externalization for things like onnxruntime-node, sharp, and tesseract.js, plus handle worker files like the sqlite snapshot worker that get referenced by path. On the TypeScript side, I'm debating how strict to be given the scale of converting thousands of lines of JS, especially since later refactoring steps will retype much of it anyway—this is shaping up to be a genuinely massive PR given the "one request, one PR" constraint.

Given the scope, I should start pragmatically by surveying the whole codebase first—checking the file tree, tsconfig, existing tests, CI workflows, the electron-builder config, and the knip config before committing to an approach.

I'm weighing whether to keep source files as .ts and compile them per entry point (main, preload, workers) into dist/electron, which would mean the dev workflow needs a build step before launching electron. I also need to figure out native dependency externalization for things like onnxruntime-node, sharp, and tesseract.js, plus handle worker files like the sqlite snapshot worker that get referenced by path. On the TypeScript side, I'm debating how strict to be given the scale of converting thousands of lines of JS, especially since later refactoring steps will retype much of it anyway—this is shaping up to be a genuinely massive PR given the "one request, one PR" constraint.

Given the scope, I should start pragmatically by surveying the whole codebase first—checking the file tree, tsconfig, existing tests, CI workflows, the electron-builder config, and the knip config before committing to an approach.

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
    paths-ignore:
      # Docs carry no executable code — skip CI entirely
      # when a push only touches these (mixed code+docs pushes still run).
      # Automation config (.entire/) is deliberately NOT ignored: runner
      # prompts execute in automation, so those changes must run checks.
      - "**/*.md"
      - "docs/**"
      - "AGENTS.md"
  pull_request:
    paths-ignore:
      - "**/*.md"
      - "docs/**"
      - "AGENTS.md"

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  changes:
    name: Detect changes
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: read
    outputs:
      frontend: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.frontend }}
    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}
          # Full history so the path filter diffs the real change set.
          # A shallow checkout can yield an empty diff and silently skip jobs.
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Filter changed paths
        id: filter
        # Pinned to the v4 tag commit: this job gates security checks, so a
        # hijacked floating tag must not be able to falsify filter outputs.
        uses: dorny/paths-filter@ceb8a2b8f2d89434be7ff52d3de7ec3738c5cc9d # v4.0.3
        with:
          # For PR synchronize events, compare only the newest push with the
          # previous head. The default PR diff compares the whole PR to main,
          # which makes a docs-only follow-up rerun code checks.
          token: ''
          base: ${{ github.event.before || github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}
          predicate-quantifier: some-with-excludes
          filters: |
            frontend:
              - 'src/**'
              - 'public/**'
              - '!src/seedPersonal.ts'
              - '!public/seed-demo/**'
              - 'benchmarks/**'
              - 'electron/**'
              - 'scripts/**'
              - '.vscode/**'
              - '*.json'
              - '*.jsonc'
              - 't3.json'
              # Workspaces the root tsconfig does not cover.
              - 'extension/**'
              - 'packages/**'
              - '!packages/**/node_modules/**'
              - 'index.html'
              - 'package.json'
              - 'bun.lock'
              - '.bun-version'
              - 'vite.config.ts'
              - 'knip.json'
              - 'biome.jsonc'
              - 'tsconfig.json'
              - 'tsconfig.node.json'
              - '.github/workflows/ci.yml'

  frontend:
    name: Frontend checks
    needs: changes
    if: needs.changes.outputs.frontend == 'true'
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04

    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Set up Bun
        uses: oven-sh/setup-bun@v2
        with:
          bun-version-file: .bun-version

      # Guards against the three Bun pins drifting apart: .bun-version,
      # packageManager, and the Bun that setup-bun actually installed.
      - name: Verify Bun version pin
        run: bun run check:bun-version

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: bun install --frozen-lockfile

      # Root tsconfig only includes src, so the extension and shared package
      # are invisible to `bun run typecheck`. Check each workspace explicitly.
      - name: Typecheck workspaces
        run: |
          bun run typecheck
          bun run --cwd extension typecheck
          bun run --cwd packages/ingestion-shared typecheck

      - name: 'Canary: real tsc typecheck (non-blocking)'
        if: always()
        continue-on-error: true
        run: |
          bun run typecheck:tsc
          bun run --cwd extension typecheck:tsc
          bun run --cwd packages/ingestion-shared typecheck:tsc

      - name: Check documented commands exist
        run: bun run check:refs

      - name: Run unit tests
        run: bun test

      - name: Check for unused code
        run: bun run knip

      - name: Lint and format frontend
        run: bun run lint

      - name: Build frontend
        run: bun run build

      # Runs the app-mode build, whose guard fails if the committed demo seed
      # has leaked back into a shipped bundle. Without this the exclusion is
      # only checked at release time.
      - name: Build frontend for the app
        run: bun run build:app

      - name: Run ingestion smoke tests
        run: bun run ingest:smoke

      # Building the Chrome MV3 extension here catches manifest and bundler
      # regressions long before someone tries to load the unpacked directory.
      - name: Build browser extension
        run: bun run --cwd extension build
name: Electron Preview

on:
  pull_request:
    types: [labeled, synchronize, reopened]
    paths-ignore:
      - "**/*.md"
      - "docs/**"
      - "AGENTS.md"
      - "public/seed-demo/**"
      - "src/seedPersonal.ts"

permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write

concurrency:
  group: electron-preview-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  changes:
    name: Detect preview changes
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: read
    outputs:
      electron: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.electron }}
    steps:
      - name: Check out pull request head
        uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Filter changed paths
        id: filter
        uses: dorny/paths-filter@ceb8a2b8f2d89434be7ff52d3de7ec3738c5cc9d # v4.0.3
        with:
          # Compare a synchronize event with the previous head, not the full
          # PR diff. This keeps a docs/demo-only follow-up from rebuilding.
          token: ''
          base: ${{ github.event.before || github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}
          predicate-quantifier: some-with-excludes
          filters: |
            electron:
              - 'electron/**'
              - 'src/**'
              - 'public/**'
              - 'package.json'
              - 'bun.lock'
              - '.github/workflows/electron-preview.yml'
              - 'scripts/prepare-electron-models.mjs'
              - 'electron/model-manifest.json'

  build:
    name: Build Windows Electron installer
    needs: changes
    if: >-
      needs.changes.outputs.electron == 'true' &&
      github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository &&
      contains(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, 'preview:win') &&
      (github.event.action != 'labeled' || github.event.label.name == 'preview:win')
    runs-on: windows-latest
    timeout-minutes: 35

    steps:
      - name: Check out pull request head
        uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}

      - name: Cache pinned Electron models
        uses: actions/cache@v6
        with:
          path: .artifacts/electron-model-cache/models
          key: inkling-electron-models-win-${{ hashFiles('electron/model-manifest.json') }}
          restore-keys: inkling-electron-models-win-

      - name: Set up Bun
        uses: oven-sh/setup-bun@v2
        with:
          bun-version-file: .bun-version

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: bun install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts

      - name: Build Electron NSIS installer
        run: bun run build:installer

      - name: Upload Electron installer
        id: installer
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: inkling-installer-win-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}-${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
          path: |
            .artifacts/electron/*.exe

content.content:
# Effect library documentation

This documentation covers the Effect library and its related packages.

When you need to find information about Effect, use this documentation and the
Effect source code available in your environment. Avoid unrelated copies of
Effect or external documentation, as they may be outdated or incorrect.

**Note**: The examples in this documentation contain comments for illustration
purposes. In practice, you would not include these comments in your code.

## Writing `Effect` code

Prefer `Effect.gen` for inline Effect code. For reusable functions, prefer
`Effect.fn("name")` when tracing is useful and `Effect.fnUntraced` when it is not,
particularly in library implementations and hot paths. Avoid functions that only
wrap and return `Effect.gen`. Attach additional behaviour with combinators; this
style is more readable and easier to maintain than using combinators alone.

### Using Effect.gen

Use `Effect.gen` to write code in an imperative style similar to async await.
You can use `yield*` to access the result of an effect.

```ts
import { Effect, Schema } from "effect"

Effect.gen(function*() {
  yield* Effect.log("Starting the file processing...")
  yield* Effect.log("Reading file...")

  // Always return when raising an error, to ensure typescript understands that
  // the function will not continue executing.
  return yield* new FileProcessingError({ message: "Failed to read the file" })
}).pipe(
  // Add additional functionality with .pipe
  Effect.catch((error) => Effect.logError(`An error occurred: ${error}`)),
  Effect.withSpan("fileProcessing", {
    attributes: {
      method: "Effect.gen"
    }
  })
)

// Use Schema.TaggedError to define a custom error
export class FileProcessingError extends Schema.TaggedError<FileProcessingError>()("FileProcessingError", {
  message: Schema.String
}) {}
```

### Using Effect.fn and Effect.fnUntraced

When writing reusable functions that return an Effect, use `Effect.fn` or
`Effect.fnUntraced` to use the generator syntax.

Use `Effect.fn("name")` when the function should create a tracing span. Prefer
`Effect.fnUntraced` when tracing is not needed, particularly for library
implementations and hot paths.

**Avoid creating functions that only wrap and return an `Effect.gen`**.

```ts
import { Effect, Schema } from "effect"

// Pass a string to Effect.fn, which will improve stack traces and also
// attach a tracing span (using Effect.withSpan behind the scenes).
//
// The name string should match the function name.
//
export const effectFunction = Effect.fn("effectFunction")(
  // You can use `Effect.fn.Return` to specify the return type of the function.
  // It accepts the same type parameters as `Effect.Effect`.
  function*(n: number): Effect.fn.Return<string, SomeError> {
    yield* Effect.logInfo("Received number:", n)

    // Always return when raising an error, to ensure typescript understands that
    // the function will not continue executing.
    return yield* new SomeError({ message: "Failed to read the file" })
  },
  // Add additional functionality by passing in additional arguments.
  // **Do not** use .pipe with Effect.fn
  Effect.catch((error) => Effect.logError(`An error occurred: ${error}`)),
  Effect.annotateLogs({
    method: "effectFunction"
  })
)

// Effect.fnUntraced avoids tracing and stack-frame capture while still reusing
// the generator body. This is preferred for library functions that do not
// represent a useful tracing boundary.
export const validateBatchSize = Effect.fnUntraced(function*(size: number): Effect.fn.Return<number, SomeError> {
  if (!Number.isInteger(size) || size <= 0) {
    return yield* new SomeError({ message: "Batch size must be a positive integer" })
  }
  return size
})

// Use Schema.TaggedError to define a custom error
export class SomeError extends Schema.TaggedError<SomeError>()("SomeError", {
  message: Schema.String
}) {}
```

### More examples

- **[Creating effects from common sources](./ai-docs/src/01_effect/01_basics/10_creating-effects.ts)**:
  Learn how to create effects from various sources, including plain values,
  synchronous code, Promise APIs, optional values, and callback-based APIs.

## Defining schemas and domain models

All validation and domain modeling in Effect is done with `Schema`.

**AVOID using predicates or manual parsing**, instead use `Schema` to parse untrusted data and validate it.

# Effect library documentation

This documentation covers the Effect library and its related packages.

When you need to find information about Effect, use this documentation and the
Effect source code available in your environment. Avoid unrelated copies of
Effect or external documentation, as they may be outdated or incorrect.

**Note**: The examples in this documentation contain comments for illustration
purposes. In practice, you would not include these comments in your code.

## Writing `Effect` code

Prefer `Effect.gen` for inline Effect code. For reusable functions, prefer
`Effect.fn("name")` when tracing is useful and `Effect.fnUntraced` when it is not,
particularly in library implementations and hot paths. Avoid functions that only
wrap and return `Effect.gen`. Attach additional behaviour with combinators; this
style is more readable and easier to maintain than using combinators alone.

### Using Effect.gen

Use `Effect.gen` to write code in an imperative style similar to async await.
You can use `yield*` to access the result of an effect.

```ts
import { Effect, Schema } from "effect"

Effect.gen(function*() {
  yield* Effect.log("Starting the file processing...")
  yield* Effect.log("Reading file...")

  // Always return when raising an error, to ensure typescript understands that
  // the function will not continue executing.
  return yield* new FileProcessingError({ message: "Failed to read the file" })
}).pipe(
  // Add additional functionality with .pipe
  Effect.catch((error) => Effect.logError(`An error occurred: ${error}`)),
  Effect.withSpan("fileProcessing", {
    attributes: {
      method: "Effect.gen"
    }
  })
)

// Use Schema.TaggedError to define a custom error
export class FileProcessingError extends Schema.TaggedError<FileProcessingError>()("FileProcessingError", {
  message: Schema.String
}) {}
```

### Using Effect.fn and Effect.fnUntraced

When writing reusable functions that return an Effect, use `Effect.fn` or
`Effect.fnUntraced` to use the generator syntax.

Use `Effect.fn("name")` when the function should create a tracing span. Prefer
`Effect.fnUntraced` when tracing is not needed, particularly for library
implementations and hot paths.

**Avoid creating functions that only wrap and return an `Effect.gen`**.

// attach a tracing span (using Effect.withSpan behind the scenes).

  // It accepts the same type parameters as `Effect.Effect`.

    yield* Effect.logInfo("Received number:", n)

    // Always return when raising an error, to ensure typescript understands that
    // the function will not continue executing.
    return yield* new SomeError({ message: "Failed to read the file" })

  // Add additional functionality by passing in additional arguments.
  // **Do not** use .pipe with Effect.fn
  Effect.catch((error) => Effect.logError(`An error occurred: ${error}`)),

    method: "effectFunction"
  })
)

export const validateBatchSize = Effect.fnUntraced(function*(size: number): Effect.fn.Return<number, SomeError> {

    return yield* new SomeError({ message: "Batch size must be a positive integer" })
  }
  return size
})

// Use Schema.TaggedError to define a custom error
export class SomeError extends Schema.TaggedError<SomeError>()("SomeError", {
  message: Schema.String
}) {}

But then I realize backup() runs through the same connection and semaphore as other queries, meaning the Effect client holds the lock for the whole backup duration — blocking app queries during large exports, which is bad UX. So I'll keep the dedicated worker with its own connection, and just derive the correct file extension dynamically from the current module's URL so it resolves correctly whether running as `.ts` or compiled `.mjs`.

Now for Stage 2, I'm designing the Effect-based job worker: a `runJobWorker` function that loops to claim a job, run its processor alongside a heartbeat fiber that renews the lease periodically, enforces a per-kind timeout, then completes or fails the job. Instead of a polling interval with explicit pump calls, I want to use a proper wake signal (via a queue, deferred, or latch) so the worker can race between waiting for new work and its poll interval.

For interruption handling, the worker runs as a forked fiber inside the managed runtime's scope, so disposing the runtime interrupts the worker and its processor (via Effect's interrupt propagation to underlying promises). I'm thinking through what happens when a job is interrupted mid-processing — it stays in 'processing' state with its lease still active, and I need to consider how the startup recovery logic handles cases where the lease hasn't actually expired yet.

Actually, since the single-instance lock guarantees only one app process at a time, any job still marked 'processing' at startup must be orphaned, so I could safely reset all processing jobs on startup rather than relying solely on lease expiry—similar to the URL enrichment recovery. I'll keep recoverExpired but add a release-on-interrupt finalizer for cleaner handling.

I also need to think through per-kind timeouts: OCR of large PDFs can legitimately run long given multiple PSM passes across many pages, so that needs a generous timeout like 30 minutes, and embedding generation needs similar headroom since the first run downloads large models.

Now I'm setting more precise timeout budgets: enrich_url gets 2 minutes since fetch already has its own timeout, thumbnails/palette/poster get 2 minutes, ocr_image gets 10 minutes. On timeout I want the job to fail with a "timed out" message so retry semantics kick in, and the processor fiber gets interrupted—though the underlying tesseract promise can't actually be cancelled, so the worker just moves on and accepts the tesseract worker stays occupied by the stuck job.

I'm also working through converting processors into Effects: today they're async functions taking job, storage, and workerId, but under Effect they'd become functions returning an Effect with proper error and dependency types, while the heavy libraries like OCR, embeddings, PDF, and sharp remain promise-based under the hood.

For concurrency, I'll keep the two existing worker fibers partitioned by kind rather than introducing a semaphore, since that's not needed yet. Progress updates would move into an Effect-based JobContext carrying job id and worker id, exposing a progress helper.

For stage 4, I'm planning to convert LibraryStorage into a proper Library service with Effect-returning methods, split across modules for items, enrichment, search, spaces, export, import, jobs, and schema, with migrations run through SqlClient at layer build time. Each IPC command maps to a payload and success schema, and registering handlers would decode the payload with Schema before dispatching to the handler, trusting main's output without re-encoding. On the renderer side, I'm defining a typed invoke function that infers payload and success types per command name directly from the schemas, so renderer-side types stay in sync with the contracts.

I want the preload layer to be generic too: rather than hardcoding a function per command, I'd iterate over a shared list of command names and wire each to ipcRenderer.invoke with a namespaced channel, keeping that name list in a tiny contracts module free of any Effect import so the preload bundle stays lightweight.

I'm weighing whether this needs its own workspace package — leaning toward `packages/contracts` as an `@inkling/contracts` package exporting TS source directly, since bundler resolution already works this way for the shared ingestion package. I'd enforce agreement between command names and schemas using a `satisfies` type constraint, and since the renderer is untrusted, decoding payloads on the main-process side is a real security win. I still need to mirror types like StoredLibraryItem as Schema structs, with metadata modeled as a Schema.Record of string keys to unknown values.

Main doesn't need to encode or validate outputs for cost reasons — types alone should suffice, with handler return types checked for assignability against the success schema's inferred type for compile-time safety. Moving to URL ingestion, I want to look at the shared ingestion file and convert it to use Effect's HttpClient with the FetchHttpClient layer, adding timeouts and retry scheduling for transient errors like 5xx and 429 responses, while preserving a simple Promise-based `ingestUrl` facade for the smoke test and benchmark harness alongside the Effect-native version.

I need to check whether the extension and renderer import this ingestion module directly or go through the shared package, since that affects interruptibility (so fetches properly abort). Beyond that, I need to update tech-stack.md, the AGENTS.md section on where code lives and Effect patterns, the changelog, and t3.json if any build or dev scripts change as part of this work.

Then comes verification: tests, typecheck, lint, knip, the directory build, and a full app run through the verify-inkling skill using CDP and the scratch library for browser/computer-use checks. After that it's filing the PR, running the sol-loop for feedback, and babysitting the process through to merge.

For the actual implementation order: first rename to TypeScript, add types, get the build script and tests passing, confirm the app runs, and commit that stage. Then move to the contracts stage before rewriting storage, since storage types should derive from the contract schemas — so the sequence is foundational rename first, then the worker (keeping in mind its dependency on the job queue), then contracts, then storage.

To avoid redundant work, since the worker depends on a job queue that becomes SqlClient-based later, I'll reorder: do the rename stage, then storage on SqlClient including the JobQueue service, then the Effect-based worker on top, then contracts plus IPC, then the final stage. The user left the ordering up to me, so this works. Before diving in, I should check a few things — the style of storage.test.ts, url-ingestion.ts, the biome config, and the ai-jobs test file (733 lines) — to match conventions. I'll send an update and take a look at those now.

I've finished reviewing the backend (storage, jobs, capture server, OCR, PDF, embeddings, export/import). Next I'll check test style, URL ingestion, and lint/typecheck setup before finalizing the plan to convert `electron/` to TypeScript.

For interruption handling, the worker runs as a forked fiber inside the managed runtime's scope, so disposing the runtime interrupts the worker and its processor (via Effect's interrupt propagation to underlying promises). I'm thinking through what happens when a job is interrupted mid-processing — it stays in 'processing' state with its lease still active, and I need to consider how the startup recovery logic handles cases where the lease hasn't actually expired yet.

Actually, since the single-instance lock guarantees only one app process at a time, any job still marked 'processing' at startup must be orphaned, so I could safely reset all processing jobs on startup rather than relying solely on lease expiry—similar to the URL enrichment recovery. I'll keep recoverExpired but add a release-on-interrupt finalizer for cleaner handling.

I also need to think through per-kind timeouts: OCR of large PDFs can legitimately run long given multiple PSM passes across many pages, so that needs a generous timeout like 30 minutes, and embedding generation needs similar headroom since the first run downloads large models.

Now I'm setting more precise timeout budgets: enrich_url gets 2 minutes since fetch already has its own timeout, thumbnails/palette/poster get 2 minutes, ocr_image gets 10 minutes. On timeout I want the job to fail with a "timed out" message so retry semantics kick in, and the processor fiber gets interrupted—though the underlying tesseract promise can't actually be cancelled, so the worker just moves on and accepts the tesseract worker stays occupied by the stuck job.

I'm also working through converting processors into Effects: today they're async functions taking job, storage, and workerId, but under Effect they'd become functions returning an Effect with proper error and dependency types, while the heavy libraries like OCR, embeddings, PDF, and sharp remain promise-based under the hood.

For concurrency, I'll keep the two existing worker fibers partitioned by kind rather than introducing a semaphore, since that's not needed yet. Progress updates would move into an Effect-based JobContext carrying job id and worker id, exposing a progress helper.

For stage 4, I'm planning to convert LibraryStorage into a proper Library service with Effect-returning methods, split across modules for items, enrichment, search, spaces, export, import, jobs, and schema, with migrations run through SqlClient at layer build time. I'm also reconsidering the error model, since current thrown errors with raw messages cross IPC into the renderer and need a cleaner structure.

I should check whether renderer code pattern-matches on error strings like "item not found" or "invalid storage input" before deciding how to define tagged errors like StorageInputError and NotFoundError, making sure message text stays identical since tests check against it. At the IPC boundary, I'll convert these failures back into rejected Errors with the same message, treating SqlError as a preserved error rather than a defect. Since all IPC handlers already run async via runtime.runPromise, there's no sync concern, and the server's captureUrl callback can similarly invoke runtime.runPromise.

For storage.test.ts, rather than rewriting all 1249 lines around Effect internals, I'm thinking of wrapping test calls through a facade where `openTestLibrary` returns an object whose methods call runtime.runPromise under the hood — so test code just adds `await` in front of calls and switches `toThrow` assertions to `rejects.toThrow`, which is a fairly mechanical transformation across the file.

I'm also weighing whether the same promise-facade pattern should be used in main.ts for IPC handlers, generically built from contracts that define name, payload schema, and success schema, with each handler implemented as an Effect — which leads into designing the stage 3 contracts package under packages/contracts/src/ipc.

Each IPC command maps to a payload and success schema, and registering handlers would decode the payload with Schema before dispatching to the handler, trusting main's output without re-encoding. On the renderer side, I'm defining a typed invoke function that infers payload and success types per command name directly from the schemas, so renderer-side types stay in sync with the contracts.

I want the preload layer to be generic too: rather than hardcoding a function per command, I'd iterate over a shared list of command names and wire each to ipcRenderer.invoke with a namespaced channel, keeping that name list in a tiny contracts module free of any Effect import so the preload bundle stays lightweight.

I'm weighing whether this needs its own workspace package — leaning toward `packages/contracts` as an `@inkling/contracts` package exporting TS source directly, since bundler resolution already works this way for the shared ingestion package. I'd enforce agreement between command names and schemas using a `satisfies` type constraint, and since the renderer is untrusted, decoding payloads on the main-process side is a real security win. I still need to mirror types like StoredLibraryItem as Schema structs, with metadata modeled as a Schema.Record of string keys to unknown values.

Main doesn't need to encode or validate outputs for cost reasons — types alone should suffice, with handler return types checked for assignability against the success schema's inferred type for compile-time safety. Moving to URL ingestion, I want to look at the shared ingestion file and convert it to use Effect's HttpClient with the FetchHttpClient layer, adding timeouts and retry scheduling for transient errors like 5xx and 429 responses, while preserving a simple Promise-based `ingestUrl` facade for the smoke test and benchmark harness alongside the Effect-native version.

Then comes verification: tests, typecheck, lint, knip, the directory build, and a full app run through the verify-inkling skill using CDP and the scratch library for browser/computer-use checks. After that it's filing the PR, running the sol-loop for feedback, and babysitting the process through to merge.

Then move to the contracts stage before rewriting storage, since storage types should derive from the contract schemas — so the sequence is foundational rename first, then the worker (keeping in mind its dependency on the job queue), then contracts, then storage.

I'm considering whether to keep the storage module as .mjs for an intermediate commit, but realize TypeScript would fail to typecheck it without type declarations or allowJs, so I'll skip that intermediate step.

Instead I'll move straight to designing the Effect storage layer in TypeScript. I'm sketching out the error module first — defining tagged error classes like InvalidInput and NotFound, along with a broader StorageError category to cover SQL and filesystem failures — while double-checking the exact Schema.TaggedError API against the Effect v4 source.

I'm settling on three tagged error types: InvalidStorageInput and NotFound as distinct cases, plus a general StorageError for IO issues, letting SqlError pass through naturally from effect/sql. The important constraint is preserving the exact message formats tests expect, like "invalid storage input: ..." and "item not found", since these may also surface directly to users through the UI. Now I'm thinking through how an Effect failure actually propagates across the IPC boundary when handled via ipcMain.handle and runtime.runPromise.

I'm working out that in this version, runPromise likely rejects with the squashed cause (the raw error itself) rather than a wrapped FiberFailure, and since Electron just stringifies rejected errors, I need the TaggedError's message property to be set correctly via the schema field. Now I'm shifting to designing the library service API—deciding against a mega-class with mixins and instead sketching out focused per-domain services, starting with something like a LibraryPaths context service.

I'm sketching out the JobQueue service with its methods for enqueueing, claiming, and tracking job progress, plus a PubSub-based notification mechanism to replace the old callback pattern, with separate signals for update notifications and worker wakeups. Then I'm moving on to outlining the Items service with its core methods for listing, retrieving, and creating content.

I'm continuing to lay out remaining services: Enrichment for OCR and thumbnail generation, Search for embeddings and similarity queries, Spaces (which depends on Search), LibraryTransfer for export/import, Settings for onboarding state, and Schema with migration logic that runs at layer construction.

I want to keep the existing idempotent "ensure"-style migration using PRAGMA user_version rather than switching to SqliteMigrator's effect_sql_migrations table, since changing migration systems risks user data. I'll keep the openDatabase logic but run it through SqlClient, and since readImportStage needs to migrate a staged copy on a separate connection, I'll expose migrate as a reusable effect that takes any SqlClient, with a dedicated layer for the staged file. I'm weighing whether to split this into many small services (more Effect-idiomatic, testable) versus one unified Library service composing the module functions.

I'm settling on a single `Library` service assembled from per-module `make*` functions — mirroring the existing itemMethods/LibraryStorage pattern — plus a separate `JobQueue` service shared by workers and the library, since this keeps things familiar and simple for consumers who just pull the `Library` service directly.

Media dependencies get passed through a config object, so `Library.layer({ databasePath, media })` provides everything needed rather than threading individual callbacks around.

Writing layer setup code...

I realize I should double-check whether foreign_keys pragma is enabled, since the cascade delete between jobs and items depends on it — but I'll keep existing behavior unchanged rather than introduce new pragmas, and make sure the database directory is created before opening the connection.

For notifications, I'll preserve the existing pattern of enqueuing within a transaction with notify disabled, then triggering the actual notify after commit. I need to think through whether waking workers after commit could cause contention, since the worker's claim transaction would be serialized by the same connection semaphore and should simply wait rather than deadlock.

I also need to avoid forking fibers inside a transaction that then try to query the database themselves, since that could deadlock against the transaction's own connection hold, and I should keep any slow filesystem work outside transaction boundaries as the existing code does. For dynamic SQL fragments like column lists or filters, I need to use the unsafe/literal escape hatches rather than normal parameter interpolation.

For row typing I'll use the typed template to get a readonly array of rows. For detecting update/delete counts, since the raw statement result shape is uncertain, I think using `RETURNING id` is cleaner than casting an unknown result — I can count returned rows instead of relying on a changes field.

I also note that node:sqlite caches prepared statements by SQL string with a capacity and TTL, that integers default to plain numbers rather than BigInt, and that BLOB columns come back as Uint8Array, which the existing decode helper should handle.

I'm designing the notification mechanism for the job queue, thinking through whether to use a single PubSub of events versus separate channels for UI updates and worker wakeups, so workers can react specifically when new items are enqueued.

I work through a latch-based approach: a worker closes the latch before claiming, claims, and if nothing found waits on the latch (or falls back to a poll interval), while enqueue opens the latch — tracing through the ordering carefully to confirm no wakeups get lost. I also consider the edge case with multiple workers sharing one latch, where a wakeup meant for one worker's job kind could get consumed by another worker closing the latch first, causing the intended worker to miss it until the next poll.

Switching tack, I consider using a PubSub for broadcast notification instead — each worker subscribes and races taking from its subscription against a sleep timeout, looping to drain any claims before waiting again; stale notifications just cause a harmless extra claim check. I settle on PubSub being the right primitive here since it supports broadcast, and start sketching how enqueue should publish to it alongside the existing update channel.

The poll loop still acts as a safety net even with wakeups since other insert paths and idle backfills exist, so I'll keep the 5s interval despite the small per-worker query cost. For the processor interface, I'm defining a type where a processor takes a job and returns an effect requiring Library, JobQueue, and JobContext, with JobContext exposing a progress callback — simpler to pass job and ctx (workerId, progress) separately, with processors pulling Library/JobQueue from context.

For error handling, I want to catch all failures and defects (not just typed errors) using Effect.exit, succeeding to complete, failing with the squashed cause message otherwise, while letting interruption just release the job without failing it. I'll wrap processing in a timeout that produces a user-facing message like "Processing took too long and was stopped" when exceeded.

Now I'm moving to writing the storage layer code, starting with shared.ts, errors.ts, and schema.ts. For schema.ts I realize the original multi-statement db.exec approach won't translate directly to SqlClient, since node:sqlite's prepare() only accepts a single statement and errors on multiple — so I need to split the schema strings into individual statements before executing them.

Since triggers contain BEGIN...END blocks with embedded semicolons, I can't just split on semicolons naively — I'll express each statement explicitly as its own array entry instead. I also need to handle PRAGMA busy_timeout and PRAGMA user_version reads/writes via sql.unsafe since pragmas can't be parameterized.

For setupFts, I'm wrapping the FTS5 setup in a transaction using sql.withTransaction, catching failures (like FTS5 being unavailable) and falling back to returning false, relying on withTransaction to handle rollback automatically rather than manually checking db.isTransaction.

Now I'm moving on to writing the actual storage files in TypeScript, replacing the old .mjs versions. I'm starting with shared.ts, defining row types and pure helper functions, though I realize StoredItem should probably be defined in contracts first rather than duplicated here, so I'll hold off and write contracts before finalizing this file.

I'll set up the contracts package first — a package.json with exports pointing to src/index.ts, depending on effect, with tsconfig mirroring ingestion-shared. Then I'm defining command names as a const array with a derived type, plus library domain schemas like StoredLibraryItem, StoredLibraryItemDetail, and StoredLibraryCard so storage can consume these shared types.

Adding IPC contract types...

I'm also checking that type-only imports from the contracts package get erased at build time with no runtime cost, then cataloging the current command payload shapes defined in main.ts—things like storage initialization, library size queries, item retrieval, search, and similarity lookups.

Continuing through the remaining commands: space management (create, delete, update, swap positions, list items), content creation (notes, quotes, URL capture, file saves), item operations (update, archive, delete), and library export/import with timezone handling.

I'm also noting job and onboarding commands, OCR enqueueing, processing retries, pairing/capture status, directory selection, and update checks. On validation strictness, I'm deciding the schema decode at the API boundary should only check types structurally, while storage keeps its own semantic validation and specific error messages.

For optional fields I should use Schema.optional everywhere so missing or explicitly undefined values are both accepted, since optionalKey alone only tolerates missing keys—this avoids breaking existing renderer calls. I also need to confirm that struct decoding ignores excess properties by default so extra fields passed by the renderer don't cause failures.

I'm now worried that unknown-key stripping could drop fields the renderer sends that storage actually depends on, like the various optional fields in updateItem and saveFile inputs (id, bodyFormat, metadata, etc.), so I need to make sure every field storage reads is explicitly declared and marked optional where appropriate, including id for saveFile since tests may pass it. files.content:
# inkling

inkling is a home for everything worth keeping. Articles, images, screenshots, PDFs, notes, quotes, video links. An Electron desktop app for Windows, with React, TypeScript, and Vite in the frontend and Node.js and SQLite in the backend. Everything stays on the machine.

Think of it as a private visual library with semantic search as the only organizer. No folders to maintain. Save abitrary media in seconds, find it later by describing it.

## What makes inkling special

People keep things here they do not want to lose, things that are important to them, or that give them inspiration or creative ideas. These are the things that we must never compromise on.

### 1. Capture is instant and seamless

Saving must be faster than deciding where something belongs. The card appears right away. OCR, embeddings, fetching and/or indexing run in the background while the user keeps browsing or continues on with something else. A change that blocks capture on processing is a bug, no matter how correct the processing is.

### 2. Performance

Lots of apps have gotten bogged down with bad tech decisions and "slop". We regularly audit for performance regressions, often caused by passing full content over Electron IPC instead of summaries/thumbnails, rendering the card grid without virtualization, loading full assets where a thumbnail would do, blocking capture on extraction/OCR/embeddings, and running FTS + vector + Smart Space re-evaluation on every keystroke. Keep capture instant and processing in background jobs. Make sure all changes are considerate of performance impact.

### 3. Local first, forever

The library lives in SQLite on the user's disk, with files kept as assets beside it under `assets/items/<id>/`. No account, no feed, no tracking. Network is only for fetching data in a URL the user asked to save like video embed links, the one time model download, or when a user plays a video embed link but that is handled by the embed. Do not add calls home, analytics, or silent uploads.

### 4. Quiet intelligence

AI helpers stay invisible. They make search better. Never surface confidence scores, AI labels, tag correction flows, or model management chores in the main interface. Never rewrite a user title, note, or tag. When AI fails, fall back to plain metadata and text search. Our mascot is an ink-blot that stays out of the way. Calm at rest, subtly alive while work runs, sad only when capture fails. It never talks, never explains AI, never interrupts, it just chills in the background and gives some life to the app.

### 5. Visual by type

An article, a photo, a PDF, a quote and a note should not all look like generic bookmarks. Each media type gets its own card treatment and its own thumbnail. Keep it that way when adding types.

## A note on taste

Simple software that feels obvious beats impressive machinery. Do not preserve complexity just because it already exists. Do not introduce machinery because it looks architecturally impressive. Understand the real constraint, then fight for the smallest model that makes the correct behavior unsurprising.

Channel both "measure twice, cut once" and "yagni". Fight scope creep. Try to honor the dev's intent in both a minimal and realistic fashion.

The rest of this document is meant to help you navigate the codebase and make changes effectively. Think of these instructions less as "hard rules", more as "good defaults". The developer's preferences should be able to override anything here. Most work in this repo will be done by agents, sometimes remote. Be careful with data, dev servers, and anything that could damage the session you are working from.

If a rule here fights the task in front of you, say so plainly and get a human sign off before breaking it.

## Glossary

We need to be on the same page with terminology. When communicating, use this language:

- **you** means the agent reading this file and changing inkling.
- **we and maintainers** mean the people building inkling. That is who you are talking to now.
- **user** means the person using inkling, saving things and searching them later.
- **item** means one saved thing in the library, whatever its type. Data, not UI.
- **card** means how an item looks in the grid and in detail. UI, not data.
- **library** means the SQLite database plus the asset store on disk.
- **capture** means getting something into the library. Paste a URL, pick a file, drag in, paste from clipboard, screenshot, or deep link.
- **job** means one unit of background work. OCR, extraction, embeddings, indexing. Runs on a persisted queue with leases.
- **embedding** means the local vector for text or image search. Nomic text and vision share one 768-dimension space.
- **Space** means a saved search shown as a collection. Smart Spaces update themselves. Regular Spaces hold manually user curated items.
- **deep link** means the companion path into the app, `inkling://capture?url=...`.
- **preview** means `bun run dev`, the web-only look with sample data.
- **full app** means the Windows Electron desktop app with the real library, built with `bun run build:dir` or `bun run build:installer`.

## The three ways to hurt yourself

1. **Killing by pattern.** Never `pkill -f`, `pgrep | kill`, or `kill` a PID you found by matching a name, path, or worktree string. Your own agent process has this worktree's path in its argv, and this machine runs several other dev servers at once. Kill only a PID you captured at spawn, or the owner of your port after confirming it is your worktree (`Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort <port> -State Listen` and the `Win32_Process` command line on Windows, `ss -H -ltnp` and `/proc/<pid>/cwd` on Linux).

2. **Writing to the live library.** The developer's real data is the SQLite file and asset store the running app owns. Reading it is fine. Copying from it for test fixtures is good. Never start a server against it, never open it read-write, never clean it up.

3. **Baking in local paths and ports.** Never hardcode a localhost port, an absolute user path, or a machine specific model cache path into source or committed config. Preview and the full app must keep working from a fresh clone on another Windows machine. Never commit a database file, a model artifact, a downloaded embedding, or a benchmark output besides the two tracked files. Never commit a pairing secret, token, or full capture URL with real content.

## Hit every surface

The common defect here is a change that works on the path tested and is missing everywhere else. Before calling ingestion or display work done, walk this list and say which entries applied.

- **Entry points.** A behavior reachable from the Add button is usually also reachable from paste, drag and drop, clipboard, screenshot capture, and the deep link. Fixing one is not fixing the feature.
- **Capture paths.** URL, article extraction, image file, screenshot, PDF, note, quote, video link, X post, misc file. An extractor change needs a decision per path, even if the decision is not supported here.
- **Search paths.** Titles, notes, article text, OCR text, domains, authors, manual tags, derived concepts, colors, semantic similarity, dates, types. If you index a new field, say how search reaches it.
- **Card types.** Article, image, PDF, video, post, note, quote, and file, as the `ItemKind` union in `src/lib/types.ts`. Shared thumbnail logic lives in one place. Keep the set coherent.
- **Reverse states.** If you added a way in, add the way out and a way to see it. Trash needs restore. A Space needs rename and delete that keeps its items. A one way door is a bug.
- **App modes.** Preview and the full app behave differently. OCR, embeddings, and file access only run in the Electron app. Do not ship a feature that silently does nothing in one mode.
- **Docs.** Check whether the change makes existing guidance inaccurate. Apply the [documentation rules](#documentation) before adding anything.

## Dev servers

- `bun install` installs. If module resolution looks broken, check the Bun version first. It must match `.bun-version` (1.4.2). `bun run check:bun-version` says so in one line.
- `bun run dev` is the quick web look at the UI. It uses sample data and has no desktop storage or processing backend.
- `bun run dev:app` opens the Electron shell in preview mode. The renderer shows the sample library and does not call the desktop backend, so capture, OCR, embeddings, and local file access are not exercised there. Test the full backend with the packaged output of `bun run build:dir`.
- `t3.json` lists the T3 Code run scripts. Keep it up to date: whenever a package.json script is renamed or removed, or a command it runs changes, update `t3.json` in the same change.
- Ports and state come from the dev setup, not from memory. Read the actual terminal output. Do not assume a port.
- Stop what you started, by the handle you tracked. See rule 1.
- Never `Start-Sleep` (or any blocking wait) after launching a server. Start it detached, do other work, then poll its log or port. A sleep blocks you from doing anything else while you wait.

## Test data

An empty library is a bad test. Seed your run with a copy of real data instead of pointing at live state.

- Copy the database file with SQLite backup semantics so the copy is consistent even if the source app is open. A raw file copy of a live database is a corrupt copy. Bring the `-wal` and `-shm` siblings when you copy raw, or better, back up through the engine.
- Data flows one way. Into your sandbox, never back out. Copy in, never symlink. Never write your test edits back to the source.
- Bring assets only for the items your flow needs. Do not copy the whole asset store to test one card.
- The committed demo seed in `public/seed-demo/` plus `src/seedPersonal.ts` is the safe default for UI work. It shuffles with a fixed seed so the order is mixed but stable. Prefer it over real data when it covers your case.
- Never commit a copied database, a real user item, or a downloaded model. The gitignore already excludes run artifacts. Keep it that way.

## Verifying

- Smallest proof that the change works. `bun test <files>` for the tests you touched, targeted lint and typecheck for the scope you changed. The full check is `bun run check`, which mirrors the CI frontend job. Do not run it unless you changed something broad or the user asked.
- **Do not run repo-wide checks.** No full `bun test` sweep or full `tsc` unless asked. CI owns the full suite.
- A test earns its place by guarding something that breaks quietly: extraction and sanitizing, embed allowlists, OCR scoring, queue leases and recovery, migrations and persistence, asset path containment and range requests, deep link and external-format parsing, ordering and race guarantees, and `liquidGlassShape`. A test added with a bug fix stays; mark it `// regression: #NNN` if its name doesn't say so.

# inkling

inkling is a home for everything worth keeping. Articles, images, screenshots, PDFs, notes, quotes, video links. An Electron desktop app for Windows, with React, TypeScript, and Vite in the frontend and Node.js and SQLite in the backend. Everything stays on the machine.

Think of it as a private visual library with semantic search as the only organizer. No folders to maintain. Save abitrary media in seconds, find it later by describing it.

## What makes inkling special

People keep things here they do not want to lose, things that are important to them, or that give them inspiration or creative ideas. These are the things that we must never compromise on.

### 1. Capture is instant and seamless

Saving must be faster than deciding where something belongs. The card appears right away. OCR, embeddings, fetching and/or indexing run in the background while the user keeps browsing or continues on with something else. A change that blocks capture on processing is a bug, no matter how correct the processing is.

### 2. Performance

Lots of apps have gotten bogged down with bad tech decisions and "slop". We regularly audit for performance regressions, often caused by passing full content over Electron IPC instead of summaries/thumbnails, rendering the card grid without virtualization, loading full assets where a thumbnail would do, blocking capture on extraction/OCR/embeddings, and running FTS + vector + Smart Space re-evaluation on every keystroke. Keep capture instant and processing in background jobs. Make sure all changes are considerate of performance impact.

### 3. Local first, forever

The library lives in SQLite on the user's disk, with files kept as assets beside it under `assets/items/<id>/`. No account, no feed, no tracking. Network is only for fetching data in a URL the user asked to save like video embed links, the one time model download, or when a user plays a video embed link but that is handled by the embed. Do not add calls home, analytics, or silent uploads.

### 4. Quiet intelligence

AI helpers stay invisible. They make search better. Never surface confidence scores, AI labels, tag correction flows, or model management chores in the main interface. Never rewrite a user title, note, or tag. When AI fails, fall back to plain metadata and text search. Our mascot is an ink-blot that stays out of the way. Calm at rest, subtly alive while work runs, sad only when capture fails. It never talks, never explains AI, never interrupts, it just chills in the background and gives some life to the app.

### 5. Visual by type

An article, a photo, a PDF, a quote and a note should not all look like generic bookmarks. Each media type gets its own card treatment and its own thumbnail. Keep it that way when adding types.

Simple software that feels obvious beats impressive machinery. Do not preserve complexity just because it already exists. Do not introduce machinery because it looks architecturally impressive. 2. **Key Technical Concepts**

   - **Packages:** effect@4.0.6 and @effect/sql-sqlite-node@4.0.6, pinned exact.
   - **SqliteClient:**
     - Built on node:sqlite. Works under Bun (probed).
     - Uses one serialized connection guarded by a semaphore, with a prepared-statement cache.
     - Transactions start with BEGIN IMMEDIATE.
     - WAL is on by default; we plan `disableWAL: true` to keep the rollback journal.
     - Has `backup()` but no API for custom SQL functions.
     - Statements support `.raw`, which returns `{changes, lastInsertRowid}`.
   - **Effect v4 APIs (verified in the installed source):**
     - `Schema.TaggedError<X>()("Tag", {message: Schema.String})` produces a real Error whose message is preserved.
     - `Effect.runPromise` rejects with the error itself.
     - `Effect.timeout` fails with a TimeoutError ("Operation timed out after '10ms'").
     - Also available: `Context.Service<Self, Iface>()("id")` with a static layer and `.of`, `Layer.effect`, `ManagedRuntime.make(layer)`, `Effect.fn` / `Effect.fnUntraced`, `Effect.forkScoped`, `Effect.onInterrupt`, `PubSub` (unbounded, publish, subscribe, take), `Latch` (make, open, close, release, whenOpen), and `Schedule`.
     - SQL lives in `effect/sql` (`SqlClient.SqlClient`, `sql.withTransaction`). Statement helpers: `sql.literal`, `sql.in`, `sql.insert`, `sql.update`, `sql.and`, `sql.or`, `sql.csv`, `sql.join`, `sql.unsafe`.
     - The HTTP client lives in `effect/unstable/http` (FetchHttpClient).
   - **Effect AI docs** are at node_modules/effect/ai-docs/src (services, managed runtime, sql basics, http-client basics). Prefer `Effect.fn("name")`, `Schema.TaggedError`, and services.
   - **Electron:** sandboxed CJS preload, contextIsolation, `ipcMain.handle("inkling:<cmd>")`, the app:// protocol, single-instance lock.

     - Never write to the live library.
     - No hardcoded ports or paths.
     - Hit every surface.
     - Minimal comments.
     - Avoid `any`.
     - Targeted tests only; no repo-wide checks unless needed.

     - **Contracts:** `packages/contracts` (@inkling/contracts), split into `commands.ts` (names only, used by preload) and `ipc.ts` (Schemas; main decodes payloads; renderer uses `import type` only).

# Full Stop

Do the same work as `full-send`, but stop with the PR ready for the user to merge.
Never merge it.

review, and babysitting steps. An explicit "full stop" request authorizes that
work without a separate "full send" request. That includes full-send's
testing permission. A "full stop" request is the permission for the test
methods Proof needs, even when a project file says to ask first, for
example before computer use. Use those methods directly. Its merge
permission does not apply. The overrides below take precedence.

## No merging

You may commit, push, rebase, fix conflicts, and use `--force-with-lease` on
this task's branch. Never merge, enable auto-merge, enter a merge queue, push
to the default branch, bypass branch protection, or delegate those actions.

Disable existing auto-merge and remove the PR from any merge queue before
work begins; check again before each push. Report these changes. If you
cannot prevent automatic merging, report the blocker before proceeding.

## Stop at the gate

Use full-send's merge gate as the readiness check. Replace its merge and
final report steps with a handoff. Proof and review must cover the final diff;
recheck behavior changes and meaningful conflict fixes before handoff.

Fetch the target branch and check the live PR's head, base, checks, reviews,
and mergeability. Confirm it is open, not a draft, and not set to merge
without the user. If someone else merged it, report that instead.

- **Ready to merge:** the merge gate passes. Leave the PR open and unmerged.
- **Waiting for required approval:** only human approval remains. Confirm
  that this is the actual blocker.
- **Blocked:** explain what prevents readiness, what you tried, and what is
  needed. Follow full-send's rules for asking the user.

In T3 Code, call `unwatch_pull_request` before the handoff or a question.
Report the PR link, final head, verdict, proof, reviewer outcome, and remaining
risks. State whether the PR is still open and unmerged.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

Only use this tool when the user explicitly says to use a subagent, or names one of the available agent types.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Glob
tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.
